key_facts: **Actinic (senile) purpura**: benign purple patches on thin sun-damaged forearms and hands after minor trauma.
**Dermatoporosis**: chronic skin insufficiency with atrophy, purpura, stellate pseudoscars and **skin tears**.
Aggravators: anticoagulants, antiplatelets, corticosteroids (topical, oral, inhaled), SSRIs, fish oil, ginkgo.
Platelets and clotting are usually normal.
Protect skin (sleeves, padding, careful transfers); **never stop anticoagulants** just for purpura without review.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **Actinic (senile/Bateman) purpura** is benign purple-red ecchymoses on thin sun-damaged forearms and hands after minimal trauma. **Dermatoporosis** describes chronic cutaneous insufficiency — atrophy, purpura, stellate pseudoscars and **skin tears**.

ul: Chronic UV + intrinsic ageing → dermal collagen/elastin loss; vessels rupture with minor shear.
Aggravators: anticoagulants, antiplatelets, topical/oral/inhaled **corticosteroids**, SSRIs, fish oil/ginkgo/high-dose vitamin E.
Platelets and clotting are usually normal in classic actinic purpura.
**"Bruising like this means a blood disorder"**: classic actinic purpura has normal clotting; check if bruises are elsewhere.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Sun and age **thin the dermis**, so vessels lose support.

mech.t: UV and ageing reduce dermal collagen and elastin.
Small vessels rupture with minor shear.
The thin epidermis and dermis separate easily.

ul: Irregular dark-red/purple patches 1–5 cm on extensor forearms and dorsal hands; fade to brown haemosiderin.
Thin translucent wrinkled skin; stellate pseudoscars; skin tears from shear/adhesive dressings.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: Clinical at typical sites. Investigate FBC/clotting/LFTs (± INR) if purpura is on covered sites, palpable, with mucosal bleeding, systemic symptoms, new anticoagulant, or unexpected INR rise. Consider elder abuse if history/pattern mismatch.

ddx.f: Grip marks, multiple ages of bruise

ul: Protect: long sleeves, tubular forearm protectors, pad furniture, careful carer transfers; avoid harsh adhesives.
Medication review with the GP — **never stop an anticoagulant solely for actinic purpura** without discussion.
Skin tears: gently approximate, non-adherent dressings, tetanus status; refer complex wounds.

refer.t: Palpable purpura or systemic vasculitis signs.
Large unexplained bruises with rising INR.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Palpable purpura or systemic vasculitis signs.
Large unexplained bruises with rising INR.

pearls: Actinic purpura is a counselling and protection problem more than a cream problem.
Inhaled as well as topical steroids can contribute — ask.
Document skin-tear classification if using local wound pathways.

quiz.q: When should you think of Skin fragility & dermatoporosis?
quiz.a: Painless purple patches on thin sun-damaged forearms after minimal trauma in an older person.
UV and age destroy dermal support around vessels → easy shear bleeding; advanced form is dermatoporosis with skin tears.

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: Reassure, protect (sleeves, pad furniture), daily emollient and sun protection; medication review with the prescriber.
Palpable purpura, non-exposed-site bruising, mucosal bleeding or safeguarding patterns — investigate / escalate.

quiz.q: Name a red flag that needs escalation.
quiz.a: Palpable purpura or systemic vasculitis signs.
